claim: HIV Rev protein routes viral RNAs containing the Rev Response Element (RRE) through the Crm1 nuclear export pathway to the cytoplasm.
source: The HIV Rev protein routes viral RNAs containing the Rev Response Element (RRE) through the Crm1 nuclear export pathway to the cytoplasm where viral proteins are expressed and genomic RNA is delivered to assembling virions.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about HIV biology stated in the abstract, supported by the broader scientific literature on HIV.

claim: The RRE assembles a Rev oligomer that displays nuclear export sequences (NESs) for recognition by the Crm1-RanGTP nuclear receptor complex.
source: The RRE assembles a Rev oligomer that displays nuclear export sequences (NESs) for recognition by the Crm1-RanGTP nuclear receptor complex.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of Rev-RRE function, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Crm1 forms a dimer with an extensive interface that enhances association with Rev-RRE.
source: Unexpectedly, Crm1 forms a dimer with an extensive interface that enhances association with Rev-RRE and poises NES binding sites to interact with a Rev oligomer.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including EM reconstruction and binding assays.

claim: The interface between Crm1 monomers explains differences between Crm1 orthologs that alter nuclear export and determine cellular tropism for viral replication.
source: The interface between Crm1 monomers explains differences between Crm1 orthologs that alter nuclear export and determine cellular tropism for viral replication.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural findings in the context of previous functional studies on Crm1 orthologs.

claim: Only fully spliced RNAs encoding viral regulatory proteins initially reach the cytoplasm for translation.
source: Only fully spliced RNAs encoding viral regulatory proteins initially reach the cytoplasm for translation (Feinberg et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feinberg et al., 1986.

claim: Rev directs the nuclear export of unspliced and partially spliced viral RNAs by engaging the Crm1 nuclear export pathway.
source: Later in the life cycle, the regulatory protein Rev directs the nuclear export of unspliced and partially spliced viral RNAs by engaging the Crm1 nuclear export pathway typically used to transport host protein cargoes and small RNAs (Sodroski et al., 1986; Emerman et al., 1989; Felber et al., 1989; Kohler and Hurt, 2007; McCloskey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The amino terminal portion of Rev recognizes the RRE through an arginine rich motif flanked by hydrophobic domains that facilitate Rev oligomerization on the RRE.
source: The amino terminal portion of Rev recognizes the RRE through an arginine rich motif flanked by hydrophobic domains that facilitate Rev oligomerization on the RRE (Malim and Cullen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malim and Cullen, 1991.

claim: The Rev nuclear export sequence (NES), located near the carboxy terminus, recruits Crm1 in cooperation with Ran bound to GTP (RanGTP) to elicit nuclear export of viral RNAs.
source: The Rev nuclear export sequence (NES), located near the carboxy terminus, recruits Crm1 in cooperation with Ran bound to GTP (RanGTP) to elicit nuclear export of viral RNAs (Fischer et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fischer et al., 1995.

claim: Crm1 co-purified with GB1-Rev in the presence of both RanGTP and the RRE.
source: Crm1 co-purified with GB1-Rev in the presence of both RanGTP and the RRE (Figure 1B, lane 11), but showed only a weak interaction with RanGDP or without the RRE (compare lane 11 to lanes 12 and 9).
evidence: This is directly shown by the pulldown experiment in Figure 1B.

claim: The interaction between Crm1 and Rev requires a functional NES.
source: The interaction between Crm1 and Rev requires a functional NES, as GB1-Rev bearing a dominant-negative M10 mutation in the NES, Leu78Asp and Glu79Leu (Malim et al., 1989), did not bind Crm1 under any condition (lanes 17–18 and 21–24).
evidence: This is shown by the pulldown experiment with the M10 mutant in Figure 1B.

claim: The RRE enhances the Rev-Crm1 interaction.
source: Furthermore, our data directly show for the first time that the RRE enhances the Rev-Crm1 interaction, supporting the hypothesis that the Rev NES must be recognized in the proper Rev-RRE context to function (Askjaer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the pulldown data showing stronger Crm1 binding in the presence of RRE.

claim: The RRE assembles six subunits of Rev into discrete, asymmetric complexes with a total mass of 160 kD.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that the RRE assembles six subunits of Rev into discrete, asymmetric complexes with a total mass of 160 kD (Daugherty et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Rev-RRE complexes associate with two copies of Crm1 and RanQ69L.
source: When increasing amounts of Crm1-RanQ69L were added to a fixed concentration of Rev-RRE, all four components eluted in a 462 kD fraction (Figure 1C,D), corresponding to two copies of Crm1 and RanQ69L per Rev-RRE complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by size-exclusion chromatography and multi-angle laser light scattering data in Figure 1C,D and supplement.

claim: Negatively stained electron micrographs of complexes clearly show two Crm1 molecules per single particle.
source: In fact, negatively stained electron micrographs of complexes from this fraction clearly show two Crm1 molecules per single particle, compared to images of Crm1 monomers alone (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is directly shown by the EM images in Figure 1E,F.

claim: A Crm1 dimer explains the need for at least two NESs in the Rev oligomer to function.
source: A Crm1 dimer explains the need for at least two NESs in the Rev oligomer to function (Hoffmann et al., 2012), and it may also be important for efficiently transporting the RRE through the nuclear pore complex since the number of receptors required for nuclear transport scales with the size of the cargo (Ribbeck and Görlich, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dimer finding in the context of previous functional studies.

claim: The number of receptors required for nuclear transport scales with the size of the cargo.
source: and it may also be important for efficiently transporting the RRE through the nuclear pore complex since the number of receptors required for nuclear transport scales with the size of the cargo (Ribbeck and Görlich, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ribbeck and Görlich, 2002.

claim: A Crm1 monomer is thought to use a protein adaptor to export relatively small, structured RNAs.
source: A Crm1 monomer is thought to use a protein adaptor to export relatively small, structured RNAs (McCloskey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCloskey et al., 2012.

claim: The RRE is almost twice the size of host RNA cargoes.
source: In contrast, the RRE is almost twice the size of host RNA cargoes, is embedded in a much larger mRNA, and is bound to the Rev oligomer.
evidence: This is a comparison based on known sizes of RNA cargoes.

claim: Previous structures of Crm1 bound to host cargo proteins have shown monomeric binding.
source: Previous structures of Crm1 bound to host cargo proteins have shown monomeric binding, so we sought to understand how Rev-RRE organizes a Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous structural studies.

claim: Single-particle negative-stain EM and a random conical tilt method were used to generate a 3D reconstruction of the Crm1-RanGTP/Rev-RRE complex.
source: We utilized single-particle negative-stain EM and a random conical tilt method (Radermacher, 1988) to generate a 3D reconstruction of the Crm1-RanGTP/Rev-RRE complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, with reference to the technique and resulting data.

claim: Two connected bowl-shaped densities, reminiscent of the known Crm1 morphology, were observed arranged with twofold symmetry in the reconstruction.
source: In this reconstruction, we observed two connected bowl-shaped densities, reminiscent of the known Crm1 morphology (Dolker et al., 2013), arranged with twofold symmetry.
evidence: This is an observation from the EM reconstruction, with reference to known Crm1 structure.

claim: Seven residues specific to simian primates that lie outside the NES-binding site and are known to be important for Rev function and HIV biogenesis were symmetrically apposed in the arrangement of the Crm1 dimer.
source: Remarkably, seven residues specific to simian primates that lie outside the NES-binding site and are known to be important for Rev function and HIV biogenesis (Nagai-Fukataki et al., 2011; Sherer et al., 2011; Elinav et al., 2012) were symmetrically apposed in this arrangement of the Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural model, with citations to functional studies.

claim: The species-specific residues form a protein–protein interface between the Crm1 monomers.
source: This fitting suggested that the species-specific residues may form a protein–protein interface between the Crm1 monomers, and indeed, we discovered that this same interface formed a crystal contact between human Crm1 monomers in the crystal structure bound to Snurportin1 (Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural fitting and confirmed by examining the crystal structure.

claim: The same interface formed a crystal contact between human Crm1 monomers in the crystal structure bound to Snurportin1.
source: This fitting suggested that the species-specific residues may form a protein–protein interface between the Crm1 monomers, and indeed, we discovered that this same interface formed a crystal contact between human Crm1 monomers in the crystal structure bound to Snurportin1 (Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a discovery made by examining the existing crystal structure from Dong et al., 2009.

claim: A Crm1 dimer held together by the symmetric interface unambiguously fit as a rigid body into the EM map.
source: We further found that a Crm1 dimer held together by this symmetric interface unambiguously fit as a rigid body into the EM map (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by the fitting of the crystal structure into the EM density in Figure 2A.

claim: The Crm1 dimer interface was not previously noted because Crm1 was known to bind the host Snurportin1 cargo as a monomer.
source: This Crm1 dimer interface was not previously noted because Crm1 was known to bind the host Snurportin1 cargo as a monomer and was seen as a monomer in the asymmetric unit of the crystal.
evidence: This explains why the dimer interface was overlooked in previous studies.

claim: The Crm1 dimer interface buries a total surface area of 2170 Å2 in the crystal structure.
source: A detailed examination of the Crm1 dimer reveals an extensive interface that buries a total surface area of 2170 Å2 in the crystal structure (Figure 2B) and corresponds to functionally important residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Central to the interface are symmetric hydrogen bonds between Arg474 and Glu478 across the dimer (2.9 Å donor to acceptor).
source: Central to the interface are symmetric hydrogen bonds between Arg474 and Glu478 across the dimer (2.9 Å donor to acceptor; Figure 2B) and, indeed, substituting these residues decreases Rev function (Elinav et al., 2012).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and supported by functional data from citation.

claim: Substituting Arg474 and Glu478 decreases Rev function.
source: Central to the interface are symmetric hydrogen bonds between Arg474 and Glu478 across the dimer (2.9 Å donor to acceptor; Figure 2B) and, indeed, substituting these residues decreases Rev function (Elinav et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Elinav et al., 2012.

claim: Swapping murine residues for Pro411, Met412, and Phe414 results in the largest reduction in activity.
source: Consistently, swapping murine residues for Pro411, Met412, and Phe414 results in the largest reduction in activity (Sherer et al., 2011; Elinav et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sherer et al., 2011 and Elinav et al., 2012.

claim: The apparent binding constant for human Crm1 to Rev-RRE was slightly, yet significantly higher than for murine Crm1 (K1/2 = 297 ± 30 nM vs 450 ± 43 nM).
source: The apparent binding constant for human Crm1 to Rev-RRE was slightly, yet significantly (p < 0.01), higher than for murine Crm1 (K1/2 = 297 ± 30 nM vs 450 ± 43 nM), and the human protein achieved higher maximal saturation (M = 0.96 ± 0.010 vs 0.90 ± 0.016, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is measured from gel mobility shift assays shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Human Crm1 achieved higher maximal saturation than murine Crm1 (M = 0.96 ± 0.010 vs 0.90 ± 0.016).
source: The apparent binding constant for human Crm1 to Rev-RRE was slightly, yet significantly (p < 0.01), higher than for murine Crm1 (K1/2 = 297 ± 30 nM vs 450 ± 43 nM), and the human protein achieved higher maximal saturation (M = 0.96 ± 0.010 vs 0.90 ± 0.016, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is measured from gel mobility shift assays shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The Hill coefficient for human Crm1 binding to Rev-RRE was 2.49 ± 0.02 compared to 1.96 ± 0.40 for murine Crm1.
source: An interesting but puzzling difference also was observed in the cooperativity term, as measured by the Hill coefficient (h = 2.49 ± 0.02 vs 1.96 ± 0.40, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is calculated from fitting the Hill equation to binding data.

claim: Human and murine Crm1 both have similar affinities for an individual NES (Kd ≈ 6–8 µM) according to the McGhee-von Hippel model.
source: In this model, human and murine Crm1 both have similar affinities for an individual NES (Kd ≈ 6–8 µM) but human Crm1 shows more than 2-fold higher cooperativity (ω = 27.8 ± 3.4 vs 12.1 ± 3.8, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is calculated from fitting the McGhee-von Hippel model to binding data.

claim: Human Crm1 shows more than 2-fold higher cooperativity than murine Crm1 (ω = 27.8 ± 3.4 vs 12.1 ± 3.8) according to the McGhee-von Hippel model.
source: In this model, human and murine Crm1 both have similar affinities for an individual NES (Kd ≈ 6–8 µM) but human Crm1 shows more than 2-fold higher cooperativity (ω = 27.8 ± 3.4 vs 12.1 ± 3.8, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is calculated from fitting the McGhee-von Hippel model to binding data.

claim: Both human and murine Crm1 occlude three binding sites on Rev-RRE.
source: Both human and murine Crm1 occlude three binding sites (Figure 2D), consistent with the stoichiometry of a Rev hexamer harboring six NESs binding to only a dimer of Crm1 (Daugherty et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is calculated from fitting the McGhee-von Hippel model to binding data.

claim: Murine Crm1 complexes with Rev-RRE elute from size-exclusion columns with an even larger apparent size than with human Crm1.
source: Indeed, murine Crm1 complexes with Rev-RRE elute from size-exclusion columns with an even larger apparent size than with human Crm1 (Figure 2E) and display a different, elongated, hour-glass shape in class averages of negatively-stained particles (Figure 2F), suggesting that these differences in the dimer complexes may reflect observed differences in Rev-RRE binding and export activities.
evidence: This is shown by size-exclusion chromatography data in Figure 2E.

claim: Murine Crm1 complexes display a different, elongated, hour-glass shape in class averages of negatively-stained particles compared to human Crm1.
source: Indeed, murine Crm1 complexes with Rev-RRE elute from size-exclusion columns with an even larger apparent size than with human Crm1 (Figure 2E) and display a different, elongated, hour-glass shape in class averages of negatively-stained particles (Figure 2F), suggesting that these differences in the dimer complexes may reflect observed differences in Rev-RRE binding and export activities.
evidence: This is shown by EM class averages in Figure 2F.

claim: The micromolar affinities for Crm1 binding to an individual NES calculated with the McGhee-von Hippel model are consistent with previous reports.
source: The micromolar affinities for Crm1 binding to an individual NES calculated with the McGhee-von Hippel model are consistent with previous reports (Paraskeva et al., 1999; Güttler et al., 2010) and underscore the importance of the RRE for scaffolding the Rev oligomer to promote the interaction with Crm1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paraskeva et al., 1999 and Güttler et al., 2010.

claim: Murine Crm1 binds the Rev-RRE complex with an order of magnitude greater affinity than to a single NES (K1/2 = 450 nM vs Kd = 5910 nM).
source: For example, murine Crm1, with apparently weak or no interaction between Crm1 monomers, still binds the Rev-RRE complex with an order of magnitude greater affinity than to a single NES (K1/2 = 450 nM vs Kd = 5910 nM).
evidence: This is calculated from the binding data comparing complex vs. single NES binding.

claim: Increasing the local concentration of NESs in the Rev-RRE complex by appending additional NESs to Rev overcomes the defect in murine Crm1.
source: Furthermore, a recent study has shown that increasing the local concentration of NESs in the Rev-RRE complex by appending additional NESs to Rev overcomes the defect in murine Crm1 (Aligeti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aligeti et al., 2014.

claim: Extra density sits on one side of the Crm1 dimer between the two NES binding sites, corresponding to bound Rev-RRE.
source: Such extra density, which sits on one side of the Crm1 dimer between the two NES binding sites, is expected to correspond to bound Rev-RRE (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the EM reconstruction shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The location of Rev-RRE density sharply contrasts with how a host cargo, Snurportin1, binds to monomeric Crm1, where the main docking surface is on the opposite side of Crm1.
source: The location of this density sharply contrasts with how a host cargo, Snurportin1, binds to monomeric Crm1, where the main docking surface is on the opposite side of Crm1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current structure and the known Snurportin1-Crm1 structure.

claim: The observed density is too small to fully accommodate a Rev hexamer bound to RNA, likely reflecting the poor visualization of RNA in uranyl-stained images as well as conformational heterogeneity.
source: Yet, the observed density is too small to fully accommodate a Rev hexamer bound to RNA, likely reflecting the poor visualization of RNA in uranyl-stained images as well as conformational heterogeneity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) arising from the disordered carboxy-terminus of Rev where the NES is located (Daugherty et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EM density limitations, with reference to known properties of Rev.

claim: Class averages of the complex formed with GB1-tagged Rev show additional density confirming the location of Rev.
source: To be certain of the locations of Rev and the RRE in the particle, we compared class averages of the complex to those formed either with GB1-tagged Rev or with streptavidin-tagged RRE (Figure 3D). Despite heterogeneity arising from flexible linkers to the tags and from different conformations within each class, additional density was plainly visible in both tagged complexes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) with Rev and the RRE unambiguously positioned on one side of the Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is shown by EM class averages in Figure 3D and supplement.

claim: Class averages of the complex formed with streptavidin-tagged RRE show additional density confirming the location of the RRE.
source: To be certain of the locations of Rev and the RRE in the particle, we compared class averages of the complex to those formed either with GB1-tagged Rev or with streptavidin-tagged RRE (Figure 3D). Despite heterogeneity arising from flexible linkers to the tags and from different conformations within each class, additional density was plainly visible in both tagged complexes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) with Rev and the RRE unambiguously positioned on one side of the Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is shown by EM class averages in Figure 3D and supplement.

claim: Class averages from cryo-electron micrographs show extra density in the same location as Rev-RRE.
source: Class averages from cryo-electron micrographs, where RNA staining is not an issue, also show extra density in the same location (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by cryo-EM class averages in Figure 3D.

claim: This work provides the first glimpse of an assembled HIV nuclear export complex.
source: This work provides the first glimpse of an assembled HIV nuclear export complex, involving an essential HIV-host interaction between the Rev-RRE complex and Crm1.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the primary contribution of the study.

claim: The Rev-RRE particle is clearly positioned at the Crm1 dimer interface.
source: The Rev-RRE particle is clearly positioned at the Crm1 dimer interface although the extent of the interface between Rev-RRE and Crm1 is unclear beyond the Rev NES interaction because there was insufficient resolution to precisely place Rev-RRE into the reconstructed complex.
evidence: This is concluded from the EM reconstruction and fitting analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity of the Crm1/Rev-RRE interaction contributes to the lack of distinct density for Rev-RRE.
source: In addition to poor staining of the RNA, heterogeneity of the Crm1/Rev-RRE interaction contributes to the lack of distinct density for Rev-RRE and presumably results from multiple arrangements of the complex as well as peptide flexibility surrounding the Rev NESs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural limitations observed in the EM data.

claim: Models of Rev oligomers suggest that a range of oligomer conformations can interface with the Crm1 dimer.
source: Furthermore, models of Rev oligomers using combinations of Rev dimer structures free or bound to RNA suggest that a range of oligomer conformations can interface with the Crm1 dimer (Jayaraman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jayaraman et al., 2014.

claim: A portion of the RRE stabilizes an alternate conformation of the Rev dimer.
source: Because a portion of the RRE stabilizes an alternate conformation of the Rev dimer (Jayaraman et al., 2014) and the whole RRE directs Rev oligomerization (Pond et al., 2009; Fang et al., 2013; Bai et al., 2014), we anticipate that the RNA modulates the conformation of the Rev oligomer and consequently its interaction with the Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jayaraman et al., 2014.

claim: The whole RRE directs Rev oligomerization.
source: Because a portion of the RRE stabilizes an alternate conformation of the Rev dimer (Jayaraman et al., 2014) and the whole RRE directs Rev oligomerization (Pond et al., 2009; Fang et al., 2013; Bai et al., 2014), we anticipate that the RNA modulates the conformation of the Rev oligomer and consequently its interaction with the Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pond et al., 2009; Fang et al., 2013; Bai et al., 2014.

claim: The RNA modulates the conformation of the Rev oligomer and consequently its interaction with the Crm1 dimer.
source: Because a portion of the RRE stabilizes an alternate conformation of the Rev dimer (Jayaraman et al., 2014) and the whole RRE directs Rev oligomerization (Pond et al., 2009; Fang et al., 2013; Bai et al., 2014), we anticipate that the RNA modulates the conformation of the Rev oligomer and consequently its interaction with the Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on RRE effects on Rev conformation.

claim: The RRE enhances the interaction with Crm1, probably reflecting the high local concentration of Rev NESs promoted by the RRE scaffold.
source: Indeed, we observe that the RRE enhances the interaction with Crm1, probably reflecting the high local concentration of Rev NESs promoted by the RRE scaffold.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding data showing RRE-dependent enhancement.

claim: If the RRE stabilizes distinct conformations of the Rev oligomer, then the volume occupied by the Rev NES in those different states could influence the affinity for the Crm1 dimer.
source: If the RRE stabilizes distinct conformations of the Rev oligomer (Jayaraman et al., 2014), then the volume occupied by the Rev NES in those different states could influence the affinity for the Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain RRE effects on binding.

claim: HIV can evolve to fine-tune the levels of nuclear export through changes in the RRE during the course of infection within a single host.
source: Such a mechanism could explain how HIV can evolve to fine-tune the levels of nuclear export through changes in the RRE during the course of infection within a single host (Legiewicz et al., 2008; Sloan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Legiewicz et al., 2008 and Sloan et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations in Crm1 that decrease Rev-dependent export and restrict viral replication correspond to residues that form the interface between Crm1 monomers.
source: It is clear that the Crm1 dimer architecture is functionally important for HIV replication since mutations in Crm1 that decrease Rev-dependent export and restrict viral replication correspond to residues that form the interface between Crm1 monomers (Nagai-Fukataki et al., 2011; Sherer et al., 2011; Elinav et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The difference between murine and human Crm1 amplifies into a fourfold defect in nuclear export and a similar defect in translation of viral proteins.
source: The difference between murine and human Crm1 amplifies into a fourfold defect in nuclear export and a similar defect in translation of viral proteins (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the functional consequences, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: These subtle differences in binding lead to a 12-fold increase in virion production when human Crm1 is expressed in mouse cells.
source: Overall, these subtle differences in binding lead to a 12-fold increase in virion production when human Crm1 is expressed in mouse cells (Sherer et al., 2011), and even these values may underestimate the differences in an endogenous context since in these experiments human Crm1 is overexpressed in cells already containing murine Crm1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sherer et al., 2011.

claim: The Crm1 surface bound by Rev-RRE is clearly distinct from where the host cargo Snurportin1 binds.
source: The Crm1 surface bound by Rev-RRE is clearly distinct from where the host cargo Snurportin1 binds (Figure 3C) and could reflect a virus-specific interface and potential therapeutic target.
evidence: This is observed from comparing the structures in Figure 3C.

claim: The Crm1 dimer may play some role in host cell biology.
source: However, it seems more likely that the Crm1 dimer plays some role in host cell biology.
evidence: This is speculation based on the existence of the dimer interface.

claim: Previous studies have implicated the same species-specific Crm1 residues as important for binding to RanBP3.
source: Previous studies have implicated the same species-specific Crm1 residues as important for binding to RanBP3, a protein that enhances interactions of Crm1 with RanGTP and some NESs, although it is not known if a Crm1 dimer is involved (Hakata et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hakata et al., 2003.

claim: Crm1 dimerization may modulate levels of nuclear export for host mRNAs.
source: Alternatively, Crm1 dimerization may modulate levels of nuclear export for host mRNAs.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential role for Crm1 dimerization.

claim: Crm1 mediates export of a small set of mRNAs via proteins bound near their 3′ ends.
source: Crm1 mediates export of a small set of mRNAs via proteins bound near their 3′ ends (Brennan et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2001; Culjkovic et al., 2006; Prechtel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: HuR forms an oligomeric complex at its 3′ RNA element.
source: One of these proteins, HuR, even forms an oligomeric complex at its 3′ RNA element (Fialcowitz-White et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fialcowitz-White et al., 2007.

claim: The HuR oligomer may also bind a Crm1 dimer, analogous to Rev.
source: Perhaps analogous to the Rev, the HuR oligomer may also bind a Crm1 dimer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarity to Rev-RRE.

claim: The positioning of cis-acting elements within a cellular mRNA may define a topology for RNA-binding proteins to recruit a Crm1 dimer without homooligomeric assemblies of proteins.
source: Moreover, the positioning of cis-acting elements within a cellular mRNA may define a topology for RNA-binding proteins to recruit a Crm1 dimer without homooligomeric assemblies of proteins.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism for Crm1 dimer recruitment.

claim: Such a mechanism would allow Crm1-mediated export to integrate different protein signals to tune the levels of nuclear export for a given mRNA.
source: Such a mechanism would allow Crm1-mediated export to integrate different protein signals to tune the levels of nuclear export for a given mRNA.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of Crm1 dimerization.

claim: The final resolution of the EM reconstruction was estimated to be 25 Å (FSC = 0.143) to 30 Å (FSC = 0.5).
source: The final resolution was estimated to be 25 Å (FSC = 0.143) to 30 Å (FSC = 0.5) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is determined from Fourier shell correlation analysis shown in the supplement.

claim: RanGTP is absent in the human Crm1 crystal structure.
source: To place Crm1 into the reconstruction, we initially fit the crystal structure of two murine Crm1-RanGTP monomers (Güttler et al., 2010) into the EM density (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), even though our complex was assembled with the human receptor, because RanGTP is absent in the human Crm1 crystal structure (Dong et al., 2009) and is known to bind on the interior of Crm1 and stabilize a strained conformation that opens the hydrophobic NES binding cleft (Monecke et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the existing crystal structure from Dong et al., 2009.

claim: RanGTP is known to bind on the interior of Crm1 and stabilize a strained conformation that opens the hydrophobic NES binding cleft.
source: To place Crm1 into the reconstruction, we initially fit the crystal structure of two murine Crm1-RanGTP monomers (Güttler et al., 2010) into the EM density (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), even though our complex was assembled with the human receptor, because RanGTP is absent in the human Crm1 crystal structure (Dong et al., 2009) and is known to bind on the interior of Crm1 and stabilize a strained conformation that opens the hydrophobic NES binding cleft (Monecke et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Monecke et al., 2009, 2013.

claim: The simian primate lineage might have acquired mutations that stabilize the Crm1 dimer interface, whereas the murine lineage might have accrued mutations that destabilize the interface.
source: This work proposed an intriguing evolutionary path for Crm1 starting from an ancestral sequence that lacked the full set of residues that we now know form the Crm1 dimer interface. The simian primate lineage might have acquired mutations that stabilize the interface, whereas the murine lineage might have accrued mutations that destabilize the interface.
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation based on the structural findings and comparison of orthologs.

claim: Rev oligomerization scaffolded by the RRE may have initially allowed ancestral viruses to recruit two Crm1 subunits even if an ancestral form of Crm1 did not have a dimeric interface.
source: Thus, Rev oligomerization scaffolded by the RRE may have initially allowed ancestral viruses to recruit two Crm1 subunits even if an ancestral form of Crm1 did not have a dimeric interface.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary history of the Rev-Crm1 interaction.

claim: The oligomerization of Rev-like proteins in other retroviruses may similarly facilitate binding to existing Crm1 orthologs that lack the dimeric interface.
source: The oligomerization of Rev-like proteins in other retroviruses may similarly facilitate binding to existing Crm1 orthologs that lack the dimeric interface.
evidence: This is speculation extending the findings to other retroviruses.

claim: Human Crm1 enhances oligomerization of a Rev-like protein from Human T-cell Leukemia Virus-1.
source: The stabilization of the Rev-RRE export complex imparted by the human Crm1 dimer interface may explain how human Crm1 enhances oligomerization of a Rev-like protein from Human T-cell Leukemia Virus-1 (Hakata et al., 2003) or why it enhances the nuclear export activity of Rev for other lentiviruses, such as feline immunodeficiency virus (Elinav et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hakata et al., 2003.
